edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential reporting. Returning stories without a substantive new development have not been carried forward. Danish reporting is translated into English while preserving attribution and uncertainty.

content.headline: Oregon teacher and father intervened in school shooting that killed four
content.shortHeadline: Teacher and father intervene in Oregon school shooting
content.standfirst: Police say a teacher tried to wrest a shotgun from a 16-year-old attacker before a father shot him dead. Four people, including three children, were killed; investigators have not established a motive.

image.caption: Police say a teacher and a father intervened during the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon.

sources.originalTitle: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
Lærer tacklede gerningsmand under skoleskyderi i Oregon: Reddede liv, siger politiet

segments.body: A teacher tackled the attacker and tried to take his shotgun as he opened fire in a special educational needs classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, police say. A father who had seen the gunman enter the school then shot him. Police say the actions of both interveners helped prevent further deaths.

Four people were killed: five-year-old Rhoam Summer, 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert and two children aged eight and 11, whose families have not released their names. A seven-year-old pupil and a 54-year-old teacher were injured. Police identified the attacker as a former pupil, 16-year-old Griffin J John II, and say they are still investigating how he got the gun and what motivated the attack.

content.headline: Trump waives Russia sanctions as Ukraine says Starshield limits remain
content.shortHeadline: Trump waives Russia sanctions as Starshield limits persist
content.standfirst: Trump has blocked many sanctions in a law he signed last month, while Kyiv says military satellite access has not fully returned to normal. European leaders are discussing Ukraine’s defence and a funding gap.

image.caption: A Ukrainian soldier sets up a satellite internet system near the frontline in Donetsk.

sources.originalTitle: Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold amid deepening row with Ukraine
Trump waives several Russia sanctions as new US law takes effect
Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
Trump afviser at have begrænset Ukraines adgang til Starlink-netværk
Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
Korrespondent efter nye Trump-udtalelser: Nu er der snart ingen vej tilbage for Ukraine - og Europa

segments.body: Donald Trump has waived many sanctions, restrictions and tariffs in a new US law targeting Russia, saying the move is in the national interest. The measure, passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month, was due to take effect on Sunday. It includes sanctions on Russian officials, banks and oil shipping, and authorises tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy.

segments.title: Support and friction
segments.body: The decision comes amid a worsening dispute between Washington and Kyiv. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says access to Starshield, a military satellite service, has not yet returned to its previous speed limits. Trump denied ordering restrictions and said he was unsure whether the service had been disrupted. Reuters reported that the slowdown order came from within the White House, citing officials briefed on the matter.

At a Brussels summit, Zelenskyy asked the EU for at least €70bn for Ukraine’s defence and resilience next year. The European Commission’s president said there was a funding gap of that size, though other partners may contribute. Italy’s defence minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that limiting US support risks weakening Ukraine and prolonging the war.

perspectives.body: Italy’s defence minister argues that withholding satellite access or intelligence would signal weakness to Moscow and make a negotiated end to the war less likely. He says Italy will continue military support, although winning parliamentary approval for further deliveries may become harder.

content.headline: Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s power system echo a plan to make cities unlivable
content.shortHeadline: Russia’s strikes threaten Ukraine’s cities and power supply
content.standfirst: A Guardian investigation describes a Russian assessment of how to cripple electricity, heating and water systems. Recent strikes have hit power infrastructure, raising concerns about the coming winter, though the document’s author is unknown.

image.caption: Kyiv and Kharkiv have experienced rolling blackouts and water outages this week.

sources.originalTitle: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares

segments.body: Russian strikes on power plants and substations have caused rolling blackouts and water outages in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine. The Guardian reports that a document, said by Ukrainian intelligence to have been intercepted, sets out ways to damage energy, heating, water and sewage systems and make urban life increasingly difficult.

The document’s origin has not been established, and the Guardian says it is withholding some technical details at Ukraine’s energy ministry’s request. Ukrainian officials say Russia’s recent attacks resemble the assessment’s proposals. Experts cited by the Guardian warn that continued strikes and difficult winter conditions could mean prolonged outages; the extent of current damage and the course of the winter remain uncertain.

content.headline: Brazil reports record drop in Amazon deforestation before election
content.shortHeadline: Amazon deforestation falls by a record 41.8% in Brazil
content.standfirst: Satellite data show deforestation in the Amazon fell sharply in the year to July, while Brazil’s election campaign makes the rainforest’s future a central issue. The government credits stronger enforcement, but the longer-term direction remains contested.

image.caption: The Amazon rainforest is a major store of carbon and home to millions of species.

sources.originalTitle: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms

segments.body: Brazil’s government says deforestation in the Amazon fell by 41.8% in the year to July 2026, the largest annual drop since records began in 1988. In the Cerrado savanna, the reported fall was 23.8%. The figures come ahead of the 25 October presidential run-off between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro.

Lula pledged to end deforestation by 2030 and has increased environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging, reversing policies under Jair Bolsonaro, when forest loss rose. The government’s environment minister called the latest decline a major achievement. Flavio Bolsonaro is expected to continue his father’s policies if elected, although he has also pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.

content.headline: Three men jailed for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico
content.shortHeadline: Three men jailed for killing surfers in Mexico
content.standfirst: A court sentenced three men to 158 years and nine months each over the 2024 killings of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad. The murders were described in court as an apparent robbery.

image.caption: The sentencing follows the killings of three friends on a surfing trip in Baja California.

sources.originalTitle: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian and US surfers in Mexico

segments.body: Three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad have each been sentenced to 158 years and nine months in prison. The men were killed during a surfing trip in Baja California in 2024. Their bodies were found in a well with gunshot wounds to the head.

The killings were described as an apparent robbery of the surfers’ truck. Their mother, Debra Robinson, told the court the deaths had taken “the future we had imagined with them”. The convicted men’s full names could not be published for legal reasons. A woman who admitted involvement in the robbery was sentenced in a separate case last year.

content.headline: Australia proposes a switch to turn off social media recommendations
content.shortHeadline: Australia proposes an off switch for social media algorithms
content.standfirst: A proposed law would require platforms to offer feeds limited to accounts users follow, alongside a broader duty to protect people online. Critics question whether the rules can be enforced and whether the switch will be practical to use.

image.caption: Following-only feeds show posts from accounts a user has chosen to follow.

sources.originalTitle: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch

segments.body: The Australian government has introduced proposed laws that would require social media platforms to let users turn off recommended posts and see only content from accounts they follow. The legislation would also impose a duty of care on online services, with potential fines of up to A$100m for breaches.

segments.title: Choice and enforcement
segments.body: The proposal follows campaigning by people who say recommendation systems repeatedly served them harmful material, including eating-disorder and misogynistic content. Technology firms argue that users already have safety controls; critics of the government’s plan say it risks censorship or may be difficult to enforce. Previous attempts at following-only feeds have often been awkward to use, and Australia’s own enforcement of a separate social media age limit has faced difficulties.

content.headline: Five of Canada’s rescued belugas have died after relocation
content.shortHeadline: Five rescued Canadian belugas die after relocation
content.standfirst: Five whales and one dolphin have died since the largest transfer of captive whales sent animals from a closed Canadian park to aquariums abroad. Experts say it is too soon to judge the move, while debate continues over long-term care for captive whales.

image.caption: Marineland, the closed Canadian park from which the belugas were moved.

sources.originalTitle: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas

segments.body: Five belugas and one dolphin have died after an international operation moved animals from Marineland, a closed Canadian marine park, to aquariums in North America and Spain. The transfer followed Canada’s rejection of Marineland’s proposed sale of the whales to China over animal-welfare concerns.

Examinations found chronic inflammatory disease in two belugas that died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, as well as foreign objects in their stomachs. Experts caution that it is too early to judge the transfers, and say the animals had been living in an ageing facility. Advocates argue that coastal sanctuaries could offer another option, but such facilities have not yet been proven as a successful way to retire captive whales.

content.headline: Katie Zacharia leaves White House press secretary job after five days
content.shortHeadline: Katie Zacharia exits White House role after five days
content.standfirst: Zacharia is leaving after a widely criticised first briefing and scrutiny of her legal credentials. Her abrupt departure comes weeks before US midterm elections, with Trump yet to name a replacement.

image.caption: Katie Zacharia speaks to reporters at the White House on 13 October.

sources.originalTitle: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
Katie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretary
Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
Katie Zacharia’s five days as press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiring

segments.body: Katie Zacharia is leaving her post as White House press secretary just five days after taking the job. Her first briefing lasted 14 minutes and included questions from three reporters. She faced further scrutiny after acknowledging that she had not passed a bar exam, despite being described as an attorney by Trump and the White House.

segments.title: A difficult moment for the White House
segments.body: Trump said he had advised Zacharia to reconsider the job, and the White House later confirmed she was leaving. A BBC analysis argues that the administration loses an experienced public spokesperson at a difficult time: Republicans are facing pressure ahead of the midterms, while the president often speaks for himself and can leave aides struggling to explain his decisions.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s analysis places the departure in a wider political context, noting Republican candidates are trying to distance themselves from Trump as the midterms approach and the White House faces several controversies.

content.headline: Devon and Cornwall police apologise to nine women over abuse cases
content.shortHeadline: Police apologise to nine women over abuse investigations
content.standfirst: The force settled claims without admitting liability after women said it mishandled allegations against officers, including by promoting some despite complaints. It denies a cover-up and says it has changed its procedures.

image.caption: Devon and Cornwall police, which apologised to nine women over its handling of their reports.

sources.originalTitle: UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women

segments.body: Devon and Cornwall police have apologised to nine women and agreed to pay compensation after they said the force mishandled allegations of domestic abuse by male officers. The claims included rape, assault, threats, harassment and coercive control. The force settled the case after a two-year legal battle without admitting liability.

segments.title: The force’s response
segments.body: The women say their reports were mocked, disbelieved or poorly investigated, and allege that officers were promoted despite complaints. The force denies evidence of a cover-up or misogyny and says none of the accused officers remain in roles protecting women from male violence. It says all reports of police-perpetrated domestic abuse will now be investigated by its professional standards department.

content.headline: Palantir’s NHS role faces fresh questions over patient trust
content.shortHeadline: NHS data watchdog warns patient distrust could undermine care
content.standfirst: The National Data Guardian says concern about the company running the NHS data platform could limit its use. Palantir disputes the evidence and says the platform has supported extra operations and reduced discharge delays.

image.caption: Demonstrators protest against Palantir outside the company’s UK headquarters.

sources.originalTitle: Patient care ‘at risk because Palantir use in the NHS is not trusted’

segments.body: The National Data Guardian has warned that distrust of the supplier behind the NHS Federated Data Platform could prevent hospitals from using it widely enough to deliver its intended benefits. The platform brings hospital information together to help manage waiting lists, operating theatres and discharges. More than four in five hospital and specialist trusts have signed up.

segments.title: Benefits and concerns
segments.body: Palantir says the platform has helped deliver 117,000 extra operations and cut delays in discharging long-stay patients. The watchdog cites rising patient opt-outs and public concerns about data sovereignty. Palantir and NHS England say data remain in the UK, under NHS control, and cannot be used by the company for its own purposes. Ministers will have to decide whether to extend the contract next year.

content.headline: London robotaxis face driver protests and calls for stronger oversight
content.shortHeadline: London drivers protest as robotaxi trials expand
content.standfirst: Drivers fear autonomous taxis could threaten their livelihoods, while a London Assembly committee wants Transport for London to have more control over permits. The effects on jobs, safety and congestion remain uncertain.

image.caption: Wayve robotaxis leave the depot after the launch of passenger rides in London.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis

segments.body: Uber and autonomous-vehicle company Wayve have begun limited robotaxi services in London, with a human safety driver still on board. Drivers plan to protest outside Wayve’s base as trials expand. A London Assembly transport committee says Transport for London should have stronger powers to permit or suspend services.

segments.title: Jobs and public safeguards
segments.body: Drivers say they fear losing income and question how automated taxis will protect passengers, while transport committee members say the effects on congestion, public transport and accessibility are unclear. Wayve says the trial is being introduced in phases and could improve safety and access. Uber says drivers and autonomous vehicles can operate side by side for some time, but acknowledges the technology will affect workers and communities.

content.headline: National security adviser faces questions over wife’s Palestine Action post
content.shortHeadline: Police assess Sarah Helm’s post backing Palestine Action
content.standfirst: Police are assessing a social media post by writer Sarah Helm, whose husband is the national security adviser. The government says her views are her own; campaigners and an antisemitism group have sharply different views on the case.

image.caption: Writer Sarah Helm, whose social media post is being assessed by police.

sources.originalTitle: UK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine Action

segments.body: Police are assessing a post by writer Sarah Helm that expressed support for Palestine Action, a group proscribed under UK terror laws. Helm wrote in defence of novelist Sally Rooney, who withdrew her books from sale in the UK after raising concerns about passing proceeds to the group. Police have not said whether they will open an investigation.

segments.title: Competing demands
segments.body: Helm is married to national security adviser Jonathan Powell. Downing Street said her views do not represent the government. A free-speech group praised her, while the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for her to face the law and said Powell should distance himself from the post. Hundreds of writers have signed a letter supporting Rooney and warning about restrictions on expression.

content.headline: UK and EU seek a youth mobility deal ahead of November summit
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU talks seek easier work and study for under-30s
content.standfirst: Negotiators are exploring a compromise that could let young Britons work across the EU, with visa numbers and student fees still unresolved. Progress could unlock a wider package of post-Brexit agreements.

image.caption: Prime Minister Andy Burnham with European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.

sources.originalTitle: UK under-30s set to work in the EU again in major Brexit deal breakthrough

segments.body: The EU is working to resolve differences over a proposed youth mobility scheme that would allow under-30s to live, study and work more easily between the UK and member states. A potential compromise would make clear that Britons entering the EU under the scheme would not face restrictions on which jobs they could take.

The sides are still negotiating the number of places: the UK has sought a cap of 50,000 visas, while the EU has proposed 150,000. Tuition fees for European students studying in the UK are another sticking point. The i Paper reports that some EU states may accept delaying that issue to help secure a wider reset deal at the 20 November summit.

content.headline: Ministers weigh new job support and benefit rules for under-25s
content.shortHeadline: Under-25s may get more job support and different benefits
content.standfirst: Alan Milburn’s review is expected to recommend a different system of support for some young people out of work. It is not clear whether disability payments would be affected, and campaigners warn against sanctions that could harm disabled claimants.

image.caption: Former health secretary Alan Milburn, whose review is examining support for young people out of work.

sources.originalTitle: The new benefits system for Gen Z: Less cash and more job support
PIP claimants under 25 should lose benefits cash if they turn down work, voters say

segments.body: The Milburn review is expected to propose more intensive health and employment support for some under-25s, with benefit payments potentially reduced or made conditional on taking up support. One proposal would replace the health element of Universal Credit for some young people with a separate system. It remains unclear whether personal independence payments would be included.

segments.title: Support, sanctions and public opinion
segments.body: The review says almost half of young people not in education, employment or training reported having a disability. A poll commissioned by the 2030 Prosperity Alliance found 61% of respondents supported reducing benefits for 18- to 24-year-olds who refused reasonable work support. Mind warned that making payments conditional could cause unnecessary stress for people with mental health problems.

perspectives.body: The polling report adds a measure of public support for tighter work-related conditions, but also includes concerns from Labour MP Neil Duncan-Jordan and Mind about whether proposed work support would be reasonable and appropriate for disabled people.

content.headline: Flu season starts early as health officials urge eligible people to get jab
content.shortHeadline: Early flu rise prompts call for eligible people to get vaccinated
content.standfirst: Flu infections in the UK remain relatively low but are rising earlier than usual. Experts say that does not by itself mean a worse season is coming, and urge eligible people to take up vaccination.

image.caption: Flu and other winter viruses are starting to circulate in autumn.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: The UK flu season has begun earlier than usual, with infections rising in October, the UK Health Security Agency says. Flu activity can peak at any time from October to March, and scientists are still debating why respiratory viruses become more common in winter.

segments.title: What an early start tells us
segments.body: Experts say changes in circulating strains and the timing of flu seasons elsewhere may help explain the early rise, but it does not necessarily predict a more severe season. Health officials are urging people eligible for the NHS flu vaccine to get it as soon as possible. Flu tends to come on quickly and cause fever and muscle aches, unlike many milder colds.

content.headline: Trump portrays Greenland defence agreement as a deal that cost the US nothing
content.shortHeadline: Trump calls Greenland defence pact a deal ‘for nothing’
content.standfirst: The US president has again presented the agreement with Denmark and Greenland as a bargain, though it does not transfer sovereignty. The pact allows for two new US military bases and opens the way to a proposed missile-defence system.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally in Georgia.

sources.originalTitle: Trump om Grønlandsaftale: Nok min bedste ejendomshandel nogensinde

segments.body: Donald Trump described the US security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as an exceptionally good real-estate deal, saying the US “got Greenland for nothing”. The agreement, signed in September, allows the US to establish two new military bases in Greenland and provides for the possible installation of the Golden Dome missile-defence system.

DR’s US correspondent says Trump is trying to shape the public narrative by repeatedly calling the agreement a good deal. She stresses that it is not a purchase and does not transfer sovereignty from the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has previously said the US wants control and ownership of Greenland, citing American security.

content.headline: Danish charity warns after 68 children named in grooming and sextortion case
content.shortHeadline: Charity warns over case involving 68 children
content.standfirst: A 25-year-old man is charged with grooming and sextortion involving children aged 11 to 14, according to the indictment. A child-protection charity says it is seeing more cases involving abuse through chats and social media.

image.caption: Psychologist Mia Winther of Red Barnet says online grooming is a deeply alarming problem.

sources.originalTitle: Red Barnet om groomingsag, der har ramt 68 børn: Et ufatteligt uhyggeligt fænomen

segments.body: A 25-year-old man is charged with grooming and sextortion involving 68 children across Denmark, aged between 11 and 14. Prosecutors say he contacted children through Snapchat and a chat-roulette service and persuaded some to perform sexual acts. Not all the children have been identified. The man denies the charges.

segments.title: Advice for families
segments.body: The charity Red Barnet says its Slet Det counselling service is encountering more cases of online grooming and abuse. Psychologist Mia Winther advises parents to stay calm, show their child care and seek help if they are unsure how to respond. The trial is due to begin on Tuesday.

content.headline: North Jutland reports a rise in family doctors after years of shortages
content.shortHeadline: More family doctors in North Jutland after years of shortage
content.standfirst: The region has added 17 practising doctors in five years and expects further growth as graduates from Aalborg’s medical programme qualify. A new clinic is due to open in Frederikshavn in January.

image.caption: Doctors Padchalack and Olaf Emil Strøm are opening a clinic in Frederikshavn.

sources.originalTitle: Region har kæmpet med lægemangel i årevis – nu går udviklingen den anden vej

segments.body: North Jutland has 350 practising family doctors, 17 more than five years ago, according to new figures. A new clinic is due to open in Frederikshavn in January. The region has relied on regional clinics to cover areas where it could not recruit a doctor; six remain, compared with 29 regional and tender-run clinics in 2017.

Regional health officials say the increase reflects doctors qualifying through Aalborg’s medical programme and choosing to stay in the region. Their target is 500 practising doctors by 2035 and no regional clinics. The coming years are expected to bring more new specialists, although the region’s goal has not yet been reached.

content.headline: Volunteer heart responders reach patients a minute faster than two years ago
content.shortHeadline: Danish volunteer heart responders arrive faster
content.standfirst: New figures show volunteer responders are reaching cardiac-arrest emergencies about a minute sooner than two years ago. One man describes how rapid CPR by his wife, responders and ambulance crews helped him recover.

image.caption: Volunteer responder Claus Madsen with Jakob Hoffmann, who survived a cardiac arrest.

sources.originalTitle: Claus var med til at redde Jakobs liv. I dag har han næsten ingen mén efter hjertestop

segments.body: Volunteer heart responders are arriving at cardiac-arrest emergencies about a minute faster than they did two years ago, according to new figures. Claus Madsen was first to reach Jakob Hoffmann’s home after an alert and joined others in giving CPR until an ambulance arrived.

Hoffmann’s heart began beating again after about 40 minutes of resuscitation. More than two years later, he says he is living well with few lasting effects and credits the rapid response by his wife, the volunteers and emergency crews. He has a pacemaker, which has not detected further irregularities.

content.headline: Danish family doctors explain possible link between size and dogs’ lifespan
content.shortHeadline: Study explores why smaller dogs may live longer
content.standfirst: A study of blood samples from nearly 900 dogs found differences in cellular activity that could help explain why larger breeds often develop disease earlier. Researchers say they have not yet established why the patterns vary by size.

image.caption: A dog photographed in Denmark; researchers are studying how size relates to ageing.

sources.originalTitle: Forskere finder mulig forklaring på, hvorfor små hunde lever længere end store

segments.body: A study published in Science examined blood samples from nearly 900 dogs and found differences in cell activity between larger and smaller animals. Researchers found more activity associated with genetic errors in larger dogs, which could be linked to a higher risk of diseases such as cancer.

Veterinary professor Maja Louise Arendt of the University of Copenhagen says the results may help explain why large breeds can develop cancer earlier in life. The researchers have not determined why the cellular patterns differ by size, or whether the same processes account for the full difference in lifespan.

content.headline: Copenhagen street singer Søren Jakobsen dies aged 53
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen street singer Søren Jakobsen dies at 53
content.standfirst: Known for singing on Strøget for decades, Jakobsen was remembered as a distinctive voice and familiar presence in the city. He began performing in central Copenhagen as a child.

image.caption: Søren Jakobsen, known to Copenhageners as Sanger Søren.

sources.originalTitle: Sanger Sørens stemme sang Strøget op. Han blev 53 år

segments.body: Søren Jakobsen, known as Sanger Søren, has died aged 53, the community centre Gang i Gaden says. For decades he sang classics on Strøget, Copenhagen’s central pedestrian street. Singer and musician Kira Skov, who knew him from her own youth as a street performer, remembered him as a kind man with a voice unlike anyone else’s.

Jakobsen began singing on Strøget as a child. His brother told B.T. that Søren had started leaving home for the street when he was 12 because he wanted to perform. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said he had little but gave Copenhagen something few others could.

content.headline: EU energy prices raise concern ahead of winter, Danish commissioner warns
content.shortHeadline: EU energy costs and low gas stocks raise winter concern
content.standfirst: Gas, electricity and diesel prices have risen amid disruption to energy supplies, and EU gas storage is lower than usual. A mild winter could ease pressure, but a cold spell or further supply disruption could force action to curb consumption.

image.caption: Activists demonstrate against the EU’s use of natural gas at a summit.

sources.originalTitle: Her er graferne, der får frygten til at brede sig inden vinteren: 'Myndighederne kan blive nødt til at gribe ind'

segments.body: Energy prices across Europe have risen following the war in the Middle East and disruption to exports. Natural-gas prices are at their highest level since the winter of 2022-23, while EU gas storage has not been filled as usual ahead of winter. Diesel prices have also been hit by supply problems affecting Middle Eastern exports and Russian refineries.

segments.title: Weather and supply risks
segments.body: Jyske Bank commodity strategist Jan Bylov says a cold winter could push prices higher and leave authorities needing to limit gas use. Current forecasts point to milder weather, but disruption to production or transport could worsen the situation. The article also reports EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen’s proposal for countries to lower electricity taxes to the EU minimum.

content.headline: Struer expands phone check-ins for older residents living alone
content.shortHeadline: Struer expands health calls to older residents living alone
content.standfirst: A pilot offering calls to residents over 67 has been extended after participants received advice and follow-up support. One resident with COPD was given a breathing device after speaking with a municipal health adviser.

sources.originalTitle: Margrethe fik et opkald fra kommunen: Hvordan har du det?

segments.body: Struer municipality is expanding a pilot that calls residents over 67 who live alone or may be lonely. On Thyholm and Jegindø, 130 people accepted a call about their health and wellbeing. Municipal health advisers can offer guidance and arrange follow-up calls or home visits where needed.

One resident, Margrethe Tøstesen, who has COPD and difficulty breathing, received a PEP breathing device after her call. The municipality says the pilot’s positive results have led it to extend the service to Gimsing and Resen parishes. Older residents can also contact the health centre themselves.

content.headline: Samoa thrash France 78-4 as coach points to NRL-Super League gap
content.shortHeadline: Samoa thrash France 78-4 as coach cites NRL gap
content.standfirst: Samoa scored 14 tries in a one-sided World Cup victory, with Sua Fa'alogo crossing four times. France coach Laurent Frayssinous said the gulf between the NRL and Super League was a major factor.

image.caption: Samoa's Sua Fa'alogo scored four tries against France.

sources.originalTitle: NRL gap a factor in France defeat by Samoa, says boss

segments.body: France were overwhelmed 78-4 by Samoa in their World Cup opener, conceding five tries in the first 20 minutes. Melbourne Storm winger Sua Fa'alogo scored four after coming on as a replacement; France's only try came from Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet.

segments.title: Frayssinous points to the league divide
segments.body: France coach Laurent Frayssinous said the growing gap between the NRL and Super League was a major factor. Almost all of Samoa's squad play in the NRL, while France's team is largely made up of Super League players. He said the NRL's skill and decision-making under pressure were improving faster.

content.headline: England embrace underdog tag ahead of Rugby League World Cup opener
content.shortHeadline: England welcome underdog tag before Tonga opener
content.standfirst: Captain George Williams says England are ready for a demanding start against a Tonga side rich in NRL talent. Injuries have forced a late change to the line-up, while the team are looking to put past World Cup disappointments to use.

image.caption: England captain George Williams has been part of the side's previous two World Cup squads.

sources.originalTitle: Underdogs? We like that tag, says England captain Williams

segments.body: England captain George Williams says his side will welcome being labelled underdogs when they meet Tonga in their World Cup opener in Perth on Saturday. He expects a tough test against a team packed with NRL players, in conditions where humidity is forecast to be above 60%.

segments.title: A changed side, and unfinished business
segments.body: England have lost Morgan Smithies to injury and made a late change after Morgan Knowles was absent, with Luke Thompson replacing him in the starting line-up. Williams, part of England's last two World Cup squads, said past defeats could provide motivation. England were beaten by Samoa in the 2022 semi-final and lost the 2017 final to Australia.

content.headline: Gloucester draw with holders as Dragons win and Edinburgh lose
content.shortHeadline: Gloucester draw; Dragons win, Edinburgh lose
content.standfirst: Gloucester and Bordeaux began the Champions Cup with a 36-36 thriller. In Challenge Cup openers, the Dragons beat Perpignan without earning a bonus point, while Edinburgh's unbeaten start ended against Toulon.

image.caption: Gloucester and Bordeaux Begles drew 36-36 in their Champions Cup opener.

sources.originalTitle: Gloucester and holders Bordeaux draw thriller
Jaminet stars as Toulon beat Edinburgh in Challenge Cup
Four-try Dragons beat Perpignan - but without bonus
Former Sale Sharks lock Andrews dies at team hotel in La Rochelle

segments.body: Gloucester came back to lead twice but could not prevent a 36-36 draw with defending Champions Cup winners Bordeaux Begles. In the Challenge Cup, the Dragons recovered from a half-time deficit to beat Perpignan, while Edinburgh lost their opener to Toulon, with Melvyn Jaminet scoring twice and contributing 22 points.

segments.title: Tributes to Hyron Andrews
segments.body: The Gloucester match began with a moment of silence for Hyron Andrews, the 31-year-old former Sale lock who died at the Johannesburg Lions' team hotel before their match at La Rochelle. South African Rugby said his death was an accident after a fall; a public prosecutor in La Rochelle is investigating. The Lions said they would play in his honour.

content.headline: Jon Rahm gives up reported £75m claim to secure exit from LIV Golf
content.shortHeadline: Rahm waives reported £75m claim to leave LIV Golf
content.standfirst: The Spaniard has agreed a separation from LIV Golf and waived his claim to money reportedly left on his contract. The deal follows the league's bankruptcy filing after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing.

image.caption: Jon Rahm joined LIV Golf in December 2023 after leaving the PGA Tour.

sources.originalTitle: Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf

segments.body: Jon Rahm has waived his entire claim against LIV Golf to secure what he called a "complete economic walk-away" from the league. ESPN reported that about $100m (£75m) remained on his contract; LIV had listed him as owed $7.4m (£5.5m) for the rest of the 2026 season when it filed for bankruptcy protection in September.

segments.title: What he keeps
segments.body: Rahm will retain the rights to Legion XIII, the LIV team he captained, but cannot use the name to form a team in TGL, the indoor league launched by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy. LIV has secured the possibility of $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit as it seeks to continue with a proposed new format.

content.headline: Manchester City's appeal faces substantial hurdles, lawyer tells BBC
content.shortHeadline: Lawyer says City face substantial hurdles in appeal
content.standfirst: A lawyer says Manchester City must show a material error or serious procedural unfairness to overturn the Premier League commission's findings. City says it is innocent and argues the ruling contains material errors.

sources.originalTitle: Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

segments.body: Manchester City were found guilty of charges relating to Premier League financial-rule breaches from 2009-10 to 2017-18, including allegations that sponsorship deals were inflated by £830m. The club denies the accusations and says it has "irrefutable evidence" that the ruling contains errors of law, principle and fact.

segments.title: What the appeal must establish
segments.body: Lawyer James Severn told BBC Sport the appeal is not simply a chance to ask a new panel to overturn the verdict: City must identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness that affected the decision. Severn said the prospects could not be assessed reliably and that success would not be easy. The appeal outcome remains unresolved.

content.headline: Olympic sprinter Beth Dobbin is now bedbound for more than 22 hours a day
content.shortHeadline: Olympic sprinter Beth Dobbin speaks about life with ME
content.standfirst: Five years after competing for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics, Beth Dobbin says ME has left her largely bedbound and without independence. She spoke to raise awareness, despite knowing the interview could worsen her symptoms.

image.caption: Beth Dobbin, who represented Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics, is speaking about life with ME.

sources.originalTitle: The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day

segments.body: Dobbin, 32, says she now gets out of bed only to eat and use the bathroom, and has left her home just five times this year. She has been diagnosed with ME, a chronic, fluctuating illness that can cause severe fatigue, pain and problems with sleep and thinking. She says even conversation, light or sound can trigger a crash lasting from days to months.

segments.title: A decision to speak out
segments.body: Dobbin said a 30-minute interview could affect her health in 2027, but felt it was important to raise awareness. She described a long search for help, including waiting 22 months for an appointment with a private specialist after her British Athletics funding ended. Her family described feeling helpless; her sister planned to run the Yorkshire Marathon to raise money for ME Research UK.

content.headline: Lewis Koumas makes Liverpool history after breakthrough Champions League night
content.shortHeadline: Koumas breaks Liverpool record in Champions League win
content.standfirst: The Wales international became Liverpool's youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League match during the 6-3 win over LASK. After a first Premier League start days earlier, he says he is focused on making the most of his chance.

image.caption: Liverpool's Lewis Koumas became the club's youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League match.

sources.originalTitle: Feel-good Koumas story something for Liverpool to smile about

segments.body: Lewis Koumas, 21, scored and assisted in Liverpool's 6-3 Champions League win over LASK, becoming the club's youngest player to achieve that in the competition. His first two efforts were ruled out for offside before he scored; Steven Gerrard had previously held the record. Koumas said he wanted to build on the opportunity rather than dwell on the milestone.

segments.title: Seizing his opening
segments.body: After loans at Stoke, Birmingham and Hull, Koumas was brought into Liverpool's plans by manager Andoni Iraola during pre-season. He had made his first Premier League start against Manchester City three days before the LASK match, and said he could not sleep after missing a chance in that game. With injured forwards potentially returning, he said he knew he had to keep pushing whenever he played.

content.headline: Real Madrid demand Tebas resign after Goebbels comparison
content.shortHeadline: Real Madrid demand Tebas resign over Goebbels comparison
content.standfirst: La Liga president Javier Tebas compared Real Madrid's communications and in-house television channel to propaganda methods used by Joseph Goebbels. The club called the remarks deeply offensive and rejected his clarification.

image.caption: La Liga president Javier Tebas.

sources.originalTitle: Real demand Tebas resign over Goebbels comparison

segments.body: Real Madrid have called for Javier Tebas to resign as La Liga president and vice-president of the Spanish FA after he said the club's communications and television channel recalled propaganda methods used by Nazi Germany's Joseph Goebbels. The club called the comparison "deeply offensive" and "morally repugnant".

segments.title: Tebas's clarification rejected
segments.body: Tebas later said he was comparing techniques, not ideology. Real Madrid said that clarification did not lessen what it called the institutionally unworthy nature of his remarks. The dispute follows earlier clashes between Tebas and the club, including over Real Madrid's criticism of refereeing.

content.headline: How Fontaines D.C. went from Dublin dive bars to stadium headliners
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C.’s unlikely rise from Dublin dive bars to stadiums
content.standfirst: As the band releases Dopamine Chamber, fans and collaborators trace a rise built on songwriting, touring and radio support—not a manufactured viral moment. Their success, one supporter argues, is the mainstream coming to them.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C., with frontman Grian Chatten at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?

segments.body: Fontaines D.C. formed at Dublin’s BIMM Music Institute in 2014 and built their audience through relentless gigging, increasingly ambitious records and early champions including BBC Radio 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq. Their first album, Dogrel, reached the UK and Irish top 10 in 2019; their latest, Dopamine Chamber, arrives as they prepare for major festival slots and stadium dates.

segments.title: A route beyond the algorithm
segments.body: The band’s rise has not followed the usual viral playbook. Marketing consultant Liam Ward describes their relatively restrained social-media presence and says the fans’ online activity looks organic. Kneecap’s Mo Chara points to their music and politics, including a homelessness benefit and opposition to the genocide in Palestine, as part of their appeal. The article suggests that talent, work, support and luck all played a part.

perspectives.body: Kneecap’s Mo Chara sums up the band’s relationship with commercial success this way: “The mainstream has come to them rather than the other way round.”

content.headline: Shygirl on the work, risks and love behind her new rock-leaning album
content.shortHeadline: Shygirl turns to rock—and makes success on her own terms
content.standfirst: The London artist’s forthcoming album Swallow! takes her from club sounds towards soaring guitars, with intimacy and vulnerability at its centre. She reflects on a working-class upbringing, ambition and the limits women face in music.

image.caption: Shygirl in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top

segments.body: Shygirl says Swallow!, her second album, is an expansive rock record inspired in part by the security and vulnerability of her relationship. Its guitars and crashing drums mark a change from the hyperpop, UK garage and electronic sounds of her earlier work. She also co-directed a series of connected videos, shaped as an elliptical thriller.

segments.title: A career built through persistence
segments.body: Born Blane Muise, Shygirl grew up in south-east London, where her parents worked a range of jobs. She says their sacrifices helped drive her to make a better life through music, though success has brought “mad guilt” as well as new opportunities. She describes women as facing a persistent barrier in the industry and says she wants to work with people who welcome difference.

content.headline: Richard Thompson on songcraft, folk history and a life on stage
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson on folk, fiction and the strange life of touring
content.standfirst: The 77-year-old guitarist answers questions about his new album, his songwriting and the musicians around him. His memories range from Sandy Denny’s anxious car rides to a knife-wielding audience member who wanted “something normal”.

image.caption: Richard Thompson.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A guy held a knife to my throat and said: play something normal!’ Richard Thompson on crazy crowds, his beloved beret and Sandy Denny’s driving skills

segments.body: Richard Thompson says the characters in his songs are not necessarily portraits of himself or people he knows. “Beeswing,” often associated with folk singer Anne Briggs, also draws on stories told by a man who visited Thompson’s Suffolk home for odd jobs, as well as Sandy Denny’s sense of Briggs as a free spirit. “I need credit as a writer of fiction, too,” he says.

segments.title: On the road
segments.body: Thompson recalls touring with Denny, jamming with John Martyn and turning down approaches from the Eagles, the Animals and the Band. One Swedish performance in the 1970s stands out: an audience member held a knife to his throat and demanded that he play “something normal”. Thompson says he wondered what “normal” meant, and may have played a Buddy Holly cover.

content.headline: Weird Baile pushes Brazilian funk into grime and drill territory
content.shortHeadline: Weird Baile takes Brazilian funk to its outer limits
content.standfirst: Collected Rips 2004-2024 brings together two decades of work by four producers who strip baile funk to bass, vocals and rhythm. The result draws on British grime and drill without simply copying either scene.

image.caption: Weird Baile, whose compilation brings together productions from 2004 to 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Weird Baile: Collected Rips 2004-2024 review – a hallucinatory trip to baile funk’s outer limits

segments.body: Weird Baile began releasing its own tracks in 2017, after producers JLZ, VHOOR, Mu540 and DJ RaMeMes connected through baile funk edits on SoundCloud. Their new compilation gathers two decades of lo-fi productions, tracing a sound that pares back the Brazilian genre’s elements and brings them into contact with British dance music.

segments.title: A productive collision
segments.body: The review hears the collection at its most distinctive when it disrupts its influences: “Grime Do Weird Baile” turns the force of a Skepta and JME beat into a bouncing dance-floor track, while other pieces lean towards drill bass or dubstep. Its abrasive, deliberately sparse production makes the compilation feel both recognisable and unsettled.

content.headline: Rachel Chinouriri finds her sweet spot in pop’s messy emotions
content.shortHeadline: Rachel Chinouriri makes room for messy feelings on her second album
content.standfirst: On i think i spoke too soon, the London singer pairs brighter, more polished production with conversational songs about love, insecurity and public embarrassment. Pitchfork finds that her emotional instincts keep the album grounded.

sources.originalTitle: I think I spoke too soon

segments.body: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album keeps the alt-rock and radio-pop influences of her 2024 debut, but gives them a shinier, more synthesised finish. Pitchfork finds that the polished sound occasionally obscures her voice, especially early on, before the record settles into sharper, more individual songs.

segments.title: Humour with a pulse
segments.body: The review highlights the rom-com-like middle stretch, where arcade sounds, guitars and violin frame Chinouriri’s anxious crush songs. Tracks such as “I’m a star” and “AAAHHH!!!” let her be funny and melodramatic without losing sight of genuine insecurity. What distinguishes her, Pitchfork argues, is the emotional precision beneath the relatable-pop persona.

perspectives.body: Pitchfork’s central reservation is that the album’s smooth production can sometimes flatten Chinouriri’s vocals; it argues that the record is strongest once her distinctive, playful delivery comes forward.

content.headline: Jon Hassell’s final Pentimento album captures his unmistakable musical voice
content.shortHeadline: Jon Hassell’s final Pentimento album returns to his singular sound
content.standfirst: Built chiefly from the trumpeter’s last live performance, Music Is Invisible reshapes old and new material into a collage of tension, echo and electronic texture. The review hears a distinctive presence still anchoring the music.

sources.originalTitle: Music Is Invisible (Pentimento Volume Three)

segments.body: Music Is Invisible completes Jon Hassell’s Pentimento series, assembled by Jeff Rona from live, studio and archival recordings. Its main source is Hassell’s final London performance, in 2015, with multi-instrumentalists Rick Cox and John von Seggern. Hassell later encouraged Rona to use the recording as a foundation for new pieces; Hassell died in 2021.

segments.title: A presence in the sound
segments.body: The review describes the album’s mood as quietly tense, with Hassell’s processed trumpet remaining its centre of gravity. On “Club Gris-Gris”, the horn moves against dub-like echoes; the long closing track, “Electric Forest”, builds from talking drums, fraying trumpet and scattered electronic detail before returning to earlier material.

content.headline: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3 deepens Harlem rapper Errol Holden’s vivid portraits
content.shortHeadline: Errol Holden’s SUPREME MAGNETIC 3 digs deeper into Harlem memories
content.standfirst: The prolific rapper turns street-level memories into dense, fast-moving vignettes over shadowy production. Pitchfork calls the album an absorbing extension of a singular storytelling voice.

sources.originalTitle: SUPREME MAGNETIC 3

segments.body: Errol Holden’s third Supreme Magnetic release continues the Harlem rapper’s autobiographical writing, built from details about neighbourhoods, people and the past. On the 33-minute album, his rapid, technically dense verses sit within spacious, ominous beats, most of them produced by the returning 2000 Souls.

The review praises Holden’s ability to make fragments feel vivid and connected, from references to old New York and childhood encounters with the Five Percenters to cast-iron pans and 1990s Reeboks. It sees the album’s restless accumulation of images—not conventional song structure—as the strength of his storytelling.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set turns new songs into living standards
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance makes new songs feel lived
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo live album documents a concert that was both a musical showcase and a moment of public mythmaking. Pitchfork singles out the new material and Winter’s exposed, expressive piano playing.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Live at Carnegie Hall records Cameron Winter’s 11 December 2025 performance, released alongside Paul Thomas Anderson’s concert film. Winter, then 24, plays piano and guitar, including three previously unreleased songs. Pitchfork hears an intimate set that gives his music room to breathe, with the piano revealing a side of his musicianship less prominent in Geese.

segments.title: A performance taking shape
segments.body: The review notes that Winter sounds nervous at the beginning, then grows more assured as the concert unfolds. It praises the new songs, especially “If You Turn Back Now”, and argues that the live arrangements transform material from his solo debut into something larger and less tethered to the difficult circumstances of its creation.

content.headline: NAZA and the difficult questions of putting perpetrators on screen
content.shortHeadline: NAZA raises hard questions about films that give perpetrators a voice
content.standfirst: The documentary’s interviews with Israeli military insiders have provoked debate over whose testimony is heard and what it can reveal. A wider look at perpetrator cinema weighs its value against the risks of centring those responsible for atrocities.

image.caption: NAZA features anonymised Israeli intelligence personnel discussing the assault on Gaza.

sources.originalTitle: Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinema
NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths
Jonathan Glazer says Israel’s retaliation over NAZA ‘more venal’ than anticipated

segments.body: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, features anonymised Israeli intelligence personnel discussing their role in the assault on Gaza. The Guardian’s analysis places it in the tradition of “perpetrator cinema”, alongside The Act of Killing and Standard Operating Procedure, and asks what these films can show about the people and systems behind atrocities.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review argues that anonymity weakens NAZA’s testimony: the interviewees’ accounts are chilling, it says, but the film’s impact is diminished when no one can be persuaded to attach a name and face to them.

segments.title: The argument over access and responsibility
segments.body: The analysis notes criticism that NAZA gives perpetrators a platform while Palestinian accounts of Gaza have already been extensively documented. It also describes the Israeli government’s threats against the filmmakers and its attempt to counter the documentary with a project of its own. Jonathan Glazer, the film’s executive producer, said the response was “much more venal” than he expected.

segments.title: What the films can—and cannot—do
segments.body: These works offer no easy catharsis, the Guardian argues. Their value lies in probing how ordinary institutions and people become implicated in violence, and in making viewers confront what they would rather reject. NAZA’s interviewees describe systems used to target Hamas operatives while anticipating civilian deaths; those claims are presented by the film and its reporting, not as independently established findings in the supplied coverage.

content.headline: Fjord turns a family dispute into a debate about Norway and Romania
content.shortHeadline: Fjord’s family drama exposes a live debate in Norway and Romania
content.standfirst: Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes-winning film echoes a real child-welfare case and has divided audiences over religion, discipline and the state’s role. Its reception reveals how sharply law, public belief and personal experience can diverge.

image.caption: A scene from Cristian Mungiu’s film Fjord.

sources.originalTitle: Dogmatic Nordic liberals v eastern family values: culture-clash drama Fjord touches nerves in Norway and Romania

segments.body: Fjord echoes the 2015 case of a Romanian Pentecostal couple in Norway whose five children were removed by child-welfare authorities amid concerns about corporal punishment and religious indoctrination. The children were later returned. In Romania, Mungiu’s fictionalised film drew a large one-night audience and reopened a charged debate about the case.

segments.title: A disagreement over what the film says
segments.body: Some viewers read Fjord as a critique of dogmatic liberalism; others say it softens a moral line on corporal punishment and gives the family undue sympathy. The article stresses that Norway and Romania both prohibit corporal punishment, while beliefs and practice differ, and notes that European human-rights rulings prompted changes to Norway’s child-welfare procedures.

perspectives.body: The article’s writer reads Fjord as a warning about institutions and communities convinced of their own good intentions: any system, the writer argues, must be able to imagine that it may be wrong.

content.headline: The Face of Horror is Anna Biller’s playful tribute to Hammer films
content.shortHeadline: Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror revives Hammer-style melodrama
content.standfirst: The director of The Love Witch turns to garish colour, Gothic revenge and deadpan humour for a film inspired by a Japanese ghost story and British 1960s horror. The Guardian review finds a future cult midnight movie.

image.caption: Jonah Hauer-King and Kristine Froseth in The Face of Horror.

sources.originalTitle: The Face of Horror review – a future cult classic delights with playful spin on Hammer horror

segments.body: Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror builds a cod-medieval tale around Yotsuya Kaidan, the Japanese ghost story that has also inspired filmmakers including Takashi Miike and Hideo Nakata. Its look and tone evoke the vivid, melodramatic horror films made by Britain’s Hammer Films in the 1960s.

Jonah Hauer-King plays Edward, a knight who murders the family members opposing his marriage to Eleanor, played by Kristine Froseth. As Edward turns towards another noblewoman, supernatural revenge gathers. The review praises the film’s sustained, deadpan excess, particularly a courtly Danse Macabre scene, and predicts a future for it as a cult midnight movie.

content.headline: The adaptation does not have to be faithful to make a great film
content.shortHeadline: Why the best film adaptations often leave the book behind
content.standfirst: From The Shining to Children of Men, Louise Willder argues that adaptation is a translation between forms, not a test of fidelity. The filmmaker’s own vision may matter more than whether readers recognise their imagined version.

image.caption: A selection of films discussed in an essay on adapting books for the screen.

sources.originalTitle: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting

segments.body: Louise Willder’s argument is that neither the quality of the source nor strict loyalty to it determines whether an adaptation works. Jaws and The Godfather became screen classics; Trainspotting and The Leopard show that celebrated novels can, too. A film must find its own visual language rather than simply reproduce a book’s events.

segments.title: Taking liberties
segments.body: Willder points to Children of Men, which turns P.D. James’s novel into a dystopian thriller, and to Sally Potter’s Orlando, which reimagines Virginia Woolf’s book. She argues that reverence can make a film feel hollow, while casting and performance can make unexpected choices work. Adaptation, in the end, is also a matter of the feelings and sensations a film leaves behind.

content.headline: You Can See Everything keeps Elizabeth Holmes’ story unresolved
content.shortHeadline: Elizabeth Holmes remains an enigma in You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim follow the convicted Theranos founder before she enters prison, letting her insist that she did nothing wrong. The film turns that uneasy access into a broader question about truth and image-making.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster

segments.body: You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes, her partner and their children in the weeks before she reported to prison in 2023. Holmes, convicted of defrauding investors, maintains in conversations with Nathan Fielder that her blood-testing device worked and that she did not lie. The film offers no settled answer about whether she believes her own account.

segments.title: Access without a verdict
segments.body: BBC Culture describes the film as a comic but unsettling hall of mirrors: Fielder’s visibly sceptical reactions undercut Holmes’s claims, while another person introduced later challenges both her account and Fielder’s own position. The directors leave the central question open, turning the film into an examination of how documentary access can shape—and complicate—a public image.

content.headline: La Bola Negra links three gay lives across a century of Spanish history
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra traces gay desire and memory across Spanish history
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film connects three men’s stories across 1932, 1937 and 2017. Its ambitious form, performances and visual style have made it a major contender in early awards conversation.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows Sebastian, a conscript in Franco’s army; Carlos, a young man shut out of an exclusive club amid rumours about his sexuality; and Alberto, a historian in 2017 investigating an unexpected family inheritance. The film draws on the work of poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and connects its timelines through memory, art and repression.

segments.title: A film gaining attention
segments.body: The film won the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto Film Festival after a Cannes reception that prompted a distributor bidding war. BBC Culture notes its awards momentum and praises the ensemble, including first-time actor Álvaro Lafuente Calvo and Penélope Cruz. The article presents a best-picture nomination as a possibility, not a settled outcome.

content.headline: Klara and the Sun turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a sentimental film
content.shortHeadline: Klara and the Sun is a misjudged, sentimental AI fable
content.standfirst: Taika Waititi adapts Kazuo Ishiguro’s story of an artificial friend into a tale of love and grief. The Guardian review argues that the film’s whimsical tone weakens its ideas about artificial intelligence.

image.caption: Jenna Ortega as Klara in Klara and the Sun.

sources.originalTitle: Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental mess

segments.body: In Taika Waititi’s adaptation, Jenna Ortega plays Klara, a solar-powered artificial friend bought for Josie, a lonely teenager with an unspecified illness. The film follows Klara as she tries to understand the family and the world around her, including her belief that the sun may help Josie.

The Guardian’s review finds the film’s humour mannered and its emotional turns unearned, arguing that it says little about AI, love or grief. It contrasts the result with more persuasive screen treatments of artificial intelligence, while acknowledging that the underlying question of whether a robot can have real feelings remains difficult to dramatise.

perspectives.body: The Guardian critic’s verdict is sharply negative: Waititi’s film is described as a sentimental, laborious mess, with its whimsical tone blunting the ideas it might have explored.

content.headline: Last One Laughing adds a no-screaming rule for its Halloween special
content.shortHeadline: Last One Laughing’s Halloween special bans screams as well as laughs
content.standfirst: The comedians must keep a straight face—and now avoid shrieking—as the hit show leans into horror for a special. Its contestants and host explain why surprise, strategy and the pressure of being watched make the format work.

image.caption: Daisy May Cooper in Last One Laughing: Halloween.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween

segments.body: The Halloween special of Last One Laughing adds a new rule: contestants must not scream as well as refrain from laughing. Phil Wang says he had not realised he was a screamer until filming. The lineup includes Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Reece Shearsmith, Daisy May Cooper and Harriet Dyer, with Jimmy Carr returning as host.

segments.title: Comedy as competition
segments.body: Carr says laughs and screams draw on the same instinct for surprise, while Wang describes the show as a mix of gameshow and psychological experiment. The comics talk about tactics, the strain of staying composed and the production’s close attention to every reaction. The article says the first series became Prime Video’s biggest UK launch at the time and later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme.

content.headline: Esther Rantzen’s kindness and campaigning live on in readers’ memories
content.shortHeadline: Readers remember Esther Rantzen’s generosity and public service
content.standfirst: Guardian readers recall the late presenter’s warmth, curiosity and commitment to people who might otherwise go unheard. Their memories range from a formative television programme to her work with Childline and bereaved families.

image.caption: Esther Rantzen, a familiar figure on British television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘She asked me to lie on her feet while she did sit-ups’: your memories of Esther Rantzen

segments.body: Readers remember Esther Rantzen welcoming them into television production, encouraging a future midwife after a programme about bereavement, and bringing her energy to social-work and Childline events. Several describe her personal attention to people around her, as well as her determination to spotlight children, families and volunteers.

segments.title: A legacy in personal encounters
segments.body: The recollections also record the reach of Rantzen’s broadcasting: one reader recalls The Big Time visiting their family home, while another remembers the investigative and comic blend of That’s Life!. Together, the accounts present her legacy through both public campaigns and small acts of encouragement.

content.headline: Seven new shows to stream, from The Audacity to Nobody Wants This
content.shortHeadline: This week’s streaming picks include The Audacity and Nobody Wants This
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s guide ranges from a satire of Silicon Valley to a Halloween comedy special and a documentary about online grooming. It offers a quick route through the week’s notable new television.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The guide’s leading pick is The Audacity, Jonathan Glatzer’s comedy about tech executives and the money, therapy and dubious business practices surrounding them. The article says it aims for a Succession-like blend of comedy and horror, though it does not reach that show’s heights.

segments.title: Other choices this week
segments.body: The selection also includes a four-part Last One Laughing Halloween special, a two-part documentary about the grooming and murder of teenager Breck Bednar, a new Lupin series and a crime documentary about European police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app. The guide additionally points to the latest Nobody Wants This and a comic story about killer garden gnomes.

content.headline: Time turns a young offenders’ prison into a study of masculinity
content.shortHeadline: Time explores anger, love and masculinity in a young offenders’ prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series follows boys in a young offenders’ institution and the guards who control them. The review links their violence to isolation, damaged relationships and a prison system stripped of rehabilitation.

image.caption: David Tennant as prison officer Bobby Bailey in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The third series of Time is set in a young offenders’ institution, where boys serving sentences for serious violence live under strict confinement. The review follows prisoners including Ushindi, Peter and James, alongside prison officer Bobby, as authority and aggression shape daily life behind the gates.

segments.title: Anger in a system of isolation
segments.body: The article argues that the show connects violence to an inability to express vulnerability and to seek love. It also points to the institution’s limited provision for rehabilitation: Bobby recalls a time when prisoners had libraries, training and education, contrasted with a present in which they can be locked in their cells for most of the day. The review says the drama offers no simple fix, but shows what unchecked anger can cost.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani brings class, grief and ambition to The Party
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and making The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner leads a new drama about a working-class journalist among wealthy political circles. She discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel, losing her mother as a teenager and the changes she has seen in Hollywood.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: The Party centres on Martin, a working-class journalist played by Luke Evans, and Ben, a Tory politician played by Tom Cullen, whose friendship has a dark secret. Sarah Solemani plays Martin’s pregnant wife, Lucy, and also wrote and showran the series, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s 2017 novel.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani says she has long wanted to write about the British class system and used her research to shape the show’s political world. She also recalls performing two monologues at her mother’s hospice bed at 16, shortly before her mother died. She says the experience of grief helped drive her towards a life in theatre and television.

content.headline: Ellie Taylor on taking Strictly’s It Takes Two in a new direction
content.shortHeadline: Ellie Taylor wants It Takes Two to embrace Strictly’s silliness
content.standfirst: The comedian and presenter says she wants the spin-off to join the wider Strictly conversation while keeping its playful spirit. She also reflects on audience criticism, social anxiety and the job she hoped to land.

image.caption: Ellie Taylor, the new host of Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie Taylor on the Strictly backlash: ‘People don’t like change’

segments.body: Ellie Taylor has taken over as host of Strictly Come Dancing: It Takes Two. A former Strictly contestant, she says she wants the programme to engage with fan conversation and lean into the show’s camp, ridiculous side. Early criticism over a panel without professional dancers was answered with a panel of pros the following day.

segments.title: Learning to live with change
segments.body: Taylor auditioned for the main Saturday-night presenting role but says she is happy with It Takes Two. Asked about criticism of Strictly’s new hosts, she argues that viewers can be resistant to change and says the dancing remains central. She describes herself as an introvert who experiences social anxiety despite her frequent on-screen work.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain pause after its latest revival
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership and cancelled a planned Christmas special, leaving the long-running series without a current Doctor. Fans and television voices disagree about what went wrong, but want the show back on screen.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, the BBC has cancelled a planned Doctor Who Christmas special and ended its collaboration with Disney+. The corporation says it is seeking a new production partner through a competitive tender, but none has yet been announced. The series currently has no Doctor in place.

segments.title: What should come next?
segments.body: Fans and contributors point to several possible causes, from confusing scripts and audience decline to the expectations attached to the Disney+ deal. Comedian Frank Skinner says the show did not need a huge investment to tell a good story and worries about how long it has been kept off air. The article argues that its future should preserve the series’ capacity to change while respecting its core identity.

perspectives.body: Lifelong fan Frank Skinner’s plea is direct: the programme should be back on screen, and whoever takes it on should avoid tampering too much with its origin story.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: Quentin Tarantino returns to Graham Norton’s sofa
content.shortHeadline: Tonight’s TV guide: Tarantino, zombies and a family heist
content.standfirst: The evening listings include Quentin Tarantino discussing his new West End play, a zombie raid on the Empire State Building and a crime comedy starring Stanley Tucci. The guide also points to a film about Kate Moss sitting for Lucian Freud.

image.caption: Quentin Tarantino, appearing on The Graham Norton Show.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Quentin Tarantino makes a rare appearance on Graham Norton’s sofa

segments.body: The guide’s headline pick is Tarantino’s return to The Graham Norton Show, where he is due to discuss The Popinjay Cavalier, his West End farce starring Sacha Baron Cohen. Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan are also listed as guests, with Suede providing the music.

segments.title: More viewing choices
segments.body: Other recommendations include The Walking Dead: Dead City, in which Maggie and Negan recruit a team for a dangerous mission in New York, and Masterplan, a heist comedy starring Stanley Tucci. The guide also highlights Moss & Freud, about supermodel Kate Moss sitting for painter Lucian Freud.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic odyssey into a strange, searching game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is an unsettling Antarctic adventure with ideas to unsp
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through an Antarctic landscape of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and fragments of human language. The Guardian finds its uneven mechanics outweighed by an ambitious, unsettling whole.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: In Penguin Colony, players guide a penguin across Antarctica, following an expedition in search of an uncanny entity. The game draws on H.P. Lovecraft’s At the Mountains of Madness, but recasts the journey through a bird’s-eye view of the expedition’s human hubris, with Nazis and other horrors occupying the landscape.

segments.title: Learning to look around
segments.body: The world moves from fishing huts and snowfields to stone labyrinths, alien obelisks and crevasses. Players can switch between penguins with different abilities, while collecting words rather than conventional treasure. The review acknowledges occasional audio and control problems, but praises the game’s finale for challenging Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism and inviting a less human-centred view of the world.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake tests what a classic should look like
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time’s remake updates Hyrule without losing its shape
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s Switch 2 version adds modern controls, 4K detail and a newly orchestrated soundtrack to its 1998 landmark. The preview weighs those improvements against the risks of revising a beloved visual style.

image.caption: Link in the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time brings changes to movement, camera control and menus, alongside updated visuals and an orchestrated soundtrack. The Guardian’s hands-on preview says Link feels significantly different to control, while familiar dungeons retain the appeal of structured puzzles and exploration.

segments.title: A new look for a familiar world
segments.body: The preview questions whether the more detailed 4K presentation risks mistaking surface polish for artistic purpose, especially in Link’s glassy-eyed design. It also considers an alternative reading: former Zelda art director Takaya Imamura suggested the character’s appearance may reflect Japanese puppet theatre. The piece notes that the visual effect feels coherent in motion, even if Nintendo’s intent remains unknown.

content.headline: Could independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: A new wave of independent arcades could revive social gaming
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to keep players online, some developers are returning to shorter, focused experiences. New independent venues may offer a social alternative to playing at home.

image.caption: A video game arcade attracting a new audience.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth
