segments.body: The Guardian’s games writer sees a shift away from “forever games” towards focused experiences shaped by arcade conventions. They point to games such as Star Wars Galactic Racer and Ace Combat 8, which offer a defined play experience rather than asking players to build their lives around a persistent online world.

segments.title: A place to play together
segments.body: The article argues for arcades that curate new and classic games and build local communities, rather than simply placing old coin-ops in a bar. Games journalist Will Freeman points to smaller ventures, including London’s forthcoming NQ Japan and Pixel Bunker in Milton Keynes, as examples of a quieter shift towards expert-led venues. The hope is that arcades can restore some of gaming’s social life to high streets.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box reflects gaming’s growing price divide
content.shortHeadline: What a £350 GTA collector’s box says about gaming’s rising cost
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise set for Grand Theft Auto 6 does not include the game itself. The Guardian argues that its price reflects a wider divide between mobile players and those able to pay more for console gaming and collectibles.

image.caption: The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection merchandise box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar has announced a £350 Grand Theft Auto 6 collector’s box of merchandise, but it does not include the game or a download code. The game itself is listed at £70, making the full outlay £420 for buyers who want both. The writer, a collector of gaming memorabilia, says the price is unusually high even by special-edition standards.

segments.title: A growing divide
segments.body: The article connects the box to wider console and game price rises, arguing that high-end gaming is increasingly a luxury purchase. It cites an estimate that about 80% of players use free or low-cost mobile games, while the remaining 20% account for a disproportionate share of spending on console and PC games. The writer worries that the games they value are becoming harder to access and own physically.

content.headline: Leap hours will replace leap seconds to reduce risks to computer systems
content.shortHeadline: Leap hours to replace leap seconds and ease risks to computer systems
content.standfirst: International timekeepers have voted to let atomic and astronomical time drift further apart before making a correction. The first leap hour is not expected for thousands of years, but the change is intended to avoid disruptive one-second adjustments.

image.caption: A clock at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.

sources.originalTitle: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
Time is a-changin’: say goodbye to the leap second

segments.body: Delegates from 69 countries have voted to replace leap seconds with leap hours. From next year, coordinated universal time can drift by as much as an hour from astronomical time before a correction is needed—a threshold the sources say is unlikely to be reached for thousands of years. The aim is to reduce the risk of computer and infrastructure failures caused by minutes with 61 or 59 seconds.

perspectives.body: The Verge reports that the change was brought forward from a 2035 target to May 2027, after concern that the Earth’s changing rotation might require the first negative leap second—a correction never attempted before.

segments.title: Why the adjustment matters
segments.body: Atomic clocks underpin communications, navigation, trading systems and electricity grids, while Earth’s rotation varies. Since 1972, timekeepers have added 27 leap seconds to keep the systems aligned. The Guardian reports that some servers froze or went offline after the 2012 adjustment; officials said testing every interconnected system for a negative leap second would be costly and difficult.

content.headline: Listening to unfamiliar sounds may help people learn a new language
content.shortHeadline: A sharp ear for sound may help with language learning
content.standfirst: A study of Japanese learners of English linked stronger auditory precision with faster, more accurate pronunciation. The researchers say the findings point to listening skills as a potential focus for language teaching, though they do not establish a single best method.

image.caption: A person learning a language by listening to its sounds.

sources.originalTitle: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

segments.body: Researchers at UCL and Tohoku University studied 67 Japanese learners of English. Those better able to detect subtle differences in pitch, length and tone in non-speech sounds learned unfamiliar English vowel sounds faster and more accurately. Their brain activity also relied less on a language-processing network associated with applying familiar pronunciation patterns.

The study’s lead author, UCL professor Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, said the findings challenge the idea that some nationalities are inherently poor at languages. He argued that teaching should develop learners’ ability to hear new sounds, alongside grammar and vocabulary. Lancaster University’s Padraic Monaghan said the study underlines the importance of listening, while noting that learners vary in sound sensitivity.

content.headline: An early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one, experts say
content.shortHeadline: Early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one
content.standfirst: Flu activity is rising in the UK earlier than usual, but scientists say timing alone cannot predict the season’s severity. The mix of circulating strains, immunity and other factors will help determine what happens next.

image.caption: Winter respiratory viruses are circulating in the UK earlier than usual.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: UK flu activity is rising earlier than usual, although infection rates were still relatively low when The i Paper reported the trend. The usual peak is in December or January, but it can fall anywhere from October to March. An early start does not by itself mean a more severe season: flu also began early last year, which ended with fewer deaths than average.

segments.title: What may affect the season
segments.body: Experts point to several possible influences, including changes in circulating strains, weather and patterns of social mixing. The strains prevalent during the Southern Hemisphere’s winter can offer clues about what may arrive in the UK months later. The UK Health Security Agency is monitoring the early rise and urging people eligible for a flu vaccine to take it up; the scale and severity of this season remain uncertain.

content.headline: A longevity researcher challenges popular anti-ageing claims
content.shortHeadline: A longevity researcher questions popular anti-ageing claims
content.standfirst: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that some headline-grabbing claims about extreme lifespans, “Blue Zones” and anti-ageing treatments rest on weak evidence. The piece also reports challenges to his critique, underscoring how contested parts of the field remain.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who has written a book critiquing modern longevity research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that claims about exceptionally long-lived populations can be undermined by unreliable age records, and questions whether so-called Blue Zones have robust evidence for unusually long lifespans. He also criticises telomere-based promises and young-blood transfusions, noting that the latter have no proven clinical benefit for preventing ageing, according to the US Food and Drug Administration.

segments.title: Claims and counterclaims
segments.body: Newman’s account is a critique of longevity research, not a settled verdict on every line of study. The article includes responses: a Sharecare spokesperson said its Blue Zones programmes are scientifically validated, while a spokesperson for Dan Buettner said Newman’s work had been disproven by independent researchers. The evidence and commercial claims should therefore be distinguished from established ways to extend lifespan.

content.headline: Man accused in London hospitals ransomware attack arrested in Germany
content.shortHeadline: Suspect in London hospitals ransomware attack arrested in Germany
content.standfirst: German police have detained a Russian man accused of belonging to the Qilin cybercrime group, which attacked blood-testing provider Synnovis in 2024. The BBC says German investigators are now examining that hack; the suspect has not been convicted.

image.caption: The man accused of involvement in the Qilin cybercrime group was detained in Frankfurt.

sources.originalTitle: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested

segments.body: The 28-year-old, identified by German media as Vladimir K., is accused of being a core member of Qilin, a ransomware group alleged to have hacked thousands of organisations. German police are investigating the 2024 attack on Synnovis, which disrupted pathology services at London hospitals, cancelled operations and affected more than 10,000 appointments.

segments.title: The impact of the Synnovis attack
segments.body: King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust said a patient died unexpectedly after the attack, with a long wait for a blood-test result among several contributing factors identified in its investigation. The BBC reports that British police are also examining whether their inquiry could lead to an unlawful-killing case. The suspect is accused; no finding of guilt is reported.

content.headline: Police and child-safety groups warn online grooming is reaching younger children
content.shortHeadline: Police warn online grooming can reach children as young as five
content.standfirst: Police and child-safety organisations say grooming is taking place across social media, messaging and gaming platforms. Their advice is to keep communication open and make clear that children will not be blamed if they seek help.

image.caption: Police warn that children can be targeted for grooming on social media and gaming sites.

sources.originalTitle: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'

segments.body: Avon and Somerset Police’s child exploitation prevention officer says children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging services. The NSPCC says Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse in the year to March 2026, with TikTok and Instagram also frequently named. These figures describe counselling contacts, not the prevalence of abuse across all users.

segments.title: How adults can respond
segments.body: Police and NSPCC staff urge parents to talk with children early, listen without judgement and avoid taking away devices in a way that could make a child feel at fault. The NSPCC says children may be afraid or embarrassed to disclose abuse. A government spokesperson says legislation is being prepared to block children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices; the report also records disagreement over whether an under-16 social-media ban would be sufficient.

content.headline: England and Wales to criminalise possession of some extreme pornography
content.shortHeadline: New rules will criminalise some extreme pornography from 6 November
content.standfirst: From 6 November, new offences will cover pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation, certain incest role-play and adults pretending to be children under 16. Campaigners welcome the move but say effective enforcement by platforms and regulators remains unresolved.

image.caption: The new rules cover pornography depicting strangulation or suffocation and certain forms of incest role-play.

sources.originalTitle: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
Pornography with strangulation and incest to be banned in England and Wales next month

segments.body: The offences, applying in England and Wales, make it illegal to publish or possess specified pornographic material depicting strangulation or suffocation, sexual activity between certain relatives, or adults role-playing as children under 16. The government says publication can carry a maximum five-year prison term; maximum penalties for possession vary by category.

segments.title: Enforcement remains a question
segments.body: The rules follow a 2025 review led by Conservative peer Gabby Bertin, which raised concerns that depictions of choking could normalise sexual violence. The government says the change is not intended to criminalise harmless sexual preferences. Campaigners have welcomed the legislation but called for effective enforcement and stronger duties on platforms to remove the material; how quickly companies and regulators will act remains an open question.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports the End Violence Against Women Coalition’s call to update the Online Safety Act so platforms are required to remove the content, an enforcement demand beyond the announcement of the new offences.

content.headline: London’s robotaxi rollout raises concerns over jobs, oversight and safety
content.shortHeadline: London robotaxi rollout prompts concerns over jobs and oversight
content.standfirst: Drivers and politicians are questioning how autonomous taxis will be regulated as trials expand. London’s transport committee wants stronger powers for Transport for London, while the impact on jobs, congestion and accessibility remains uncertain.

image.caption: Wayve robotaxis leave a London depot after the launch of passenger rides through Uber.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis

segments.body: Uber and Wayve have begun limited autonomous taxi services in London with a human safety driver in the vehicle. The rollout has prompted concern from drivers about their livelihoods and from politicians about who should control future services. A London Assembly transport committee says Transport for London should have full powers to permit or suspend operations.

segments.title: Benefits and risks are disputed
segments.body: The committee says there is considerable uncertainty about claimed benefits, including effects on congestion, public transport, safeguarding and access for disabled passengers. Drivers interviewed by The Guardian fear that robotaxis could erode earnings and remove the human support they provide to passengers. Uber and Wayve say driverless services and human drivers can coexist for some time, and that the technology could improve safety and access if introduced responsibly.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting centres the drivers’ concerns and the committee’s call for local control, while also recording that the current London services retain a human safety driver.

content.headline: Electronic noses help authorities trace industrial odours to their source
content.shortHeadline: Electronic noses help trace the source of industrial odours
content.standfirst: Air monitors paired with weather data are helping officials in Des Moines link complaints to particular facilities. The approach can make investigations more precise, though odour control remains costly and smells are subjective.

image.caption: The Newby Island landfill has been ordered to take action over odours.

sources.originalTitle: Living with a stink? Technology might help

segments.body: In Des Moines, Iowa, authorities use a network of monitors to measure chemicals in the air alongside weather data, helping them identify which facilities may be responsible when odours affect neighbourhoods. Officials say the system has reduced disputes about the source of particular incidents. The city spends about $240,000 a year on the monitoring technology.

Monitoring can identify a likely source, but it does not itself remove the smell. Experts say treatment systems can remove 90% or more of targeted compounds when used correctly, but they can be expensive; some operators instead use deodorisers, whose effectiveness experts quoted in the report question. The story also describes action at a California landfill, where drones and monitors have been ordered to track odours.

content.headline: Study links problematic social-media use with health risks for young people
content.shortHeadline: Study links problematic digital-media use with health risks
content.standfirst: A Lancet series reviewing research on millions of people under 25 reports associations between problematic digital-media use and poorer mental health, sleep and physical activity. The authors say the links are not conclusive, but warrant action and better access to platform data.

image.caption: Researchers examined links between digital-media use and health outcomes for people under 25.

sources.originalTitle: Three ways social media is harming young people, according to landmark study

segments.body: A three-paper series in The Lancet reviewed research covering nine million people under 25. It found that problematic digital-media use was associated with higher risks of mental-health problems, sleep issues and reduced physical activity. The researchers described the links as modest and not conclusive, but argued they were strong enough to justify coordinated action.

segments.title: Calls for transparency and regulation
segments.body: Researchers say companies should share data so independent teams can examine how platform features affect health. The series points to features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalised recommendations as deliberate design choices, and some policy experts argue that regulation should address those features rather than rely only on age bans. The findings describe associations; they do not by themselves prove that social media use caused the outcomes.

content.headline: Fake WhatsApp app appears above the genuine one in Google Play search
content.shortHeadline: Fake WhatsApp app appears above the real one in Play Store
content.standfirst: A lookalike Android app reportedly appeared as a sponsored result above WhatsApp on Google Play and had passed 500,000 downloads. Google had not responded to a request for comment when The Verge reported the listing was still live.

sources.originalTitle: A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store

segments.body: A user reported seeing a fake app called “WhatsApp Messenger” in a sponsored slot above the genuine app in the Play Store. The clone used the real app’s icon, screenshots and text, and had more than 500,000 downloads, according to The Verge. At the time of its report, the listing remained live and Google had not responded to a request for comment.

The listing was attributed to a developer called “Agment Assets sallu”, which had no other apps listed. The genuine WhatsApp has far more downloads and reviews, but the report notes that the clone may have used Google Play’s Early Access programme, which can disable public reviews. The report does not establish what the imitation app did after installation.

content.headline: Palantir drops legal challenge over blocked Metropolitan Police contract
content.shortHeadline: Palantir settles challenge over blocked Met Police contract
content.standfirst: Palantir has settled its challenge over a proposed £50m Metropolitan Police software contract, but the deal remains blocked and is to be put out to tender again. The parties say the original decision was about procurement and value for money, not Palantir’s ethics.

image.caption: The mayor’s office blocked a proposed software contract between the Metropolitan Police and Palantir.

sources.originalTitle: Palantir and City Hall settle Met contract row

segments.body: The Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime and Palantir have settled the company’s High Court challenge to the blocking of a proposed two-year contract for software to automate intelligence analysis. The decision has not been reversed: the Met is to rerun the procurement. A joint statement said neither side paid the other and both will cover their own legal costs.

The mayor’s office said the decision was based on its duty to scrutinise spending and ensure value for money, and that a previous media statement could have wrongly suggested Palantir’s values were a factor. The Met had argued the software could help it meet a budget shortfall and warned that jobs or services might otherwise be cut. The contract’s outcome remains undecided.

content.headline: Journalist says AI-assisted impostor used her identity to sell a story
content.shortHeadline: Journalist says AI impostor used her identity to pitch a story
content.standfirst: A freelance journalist says someone pitched and sold an AI-generated article under her name, damaging her professional reputation. The person disputes impersonating her, while the publication says the pitch identified the real journalist.

image.caption: Freelance journalist Caroline Williams says a suspected impostor used her identity to pitch an article.

sources.originalTitle: My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Caroline Williams, a freelance journalist, says she discovered that Science had published an article under her name that she had not written. The i Paper reports that the piece contained copied quotes and that detection software indicated the first draft was AI-written. Science removed it and said it had paid the person who submitted it $1,000.

segments.title: The identity dispute
segments.body: The person who submitted the article told The i Paper they were a different journalist with the same name and denied impersonating Williams. But Williams and Science’s managing news editor dispute that account: the editor said the person had clearly identified themselves as the UK journalist. Science says it will speak with new writers by phone or video and use AI-detection software; Williams says she cannot know whether other editors received fake pitches in her name.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reporting includes a response from the person who submitted the article, who says the shared name was not intended to imply authorship of Williams’s previous work—a claim Williams and Science’s editor reject.

content.headline: Meta’s open-weight AI model is designed to run on Apple’s Mac Studios
content.shortHeadline: Meta releases an open-weight AI model built for powerful Macs
content.standfirst: Meta says Muse Spark Open is a large multimodal model for coding and other complex tasks, and worked with Apple to support running it on Mac Studio computers. The performance claims are the company’s; the required computing resources make local use demanding.

sources.originalTitle: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs
Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs

segments.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model it describes as its most capable US offering of that kind. The company says the multimodal model has 816 billion parameters and a one-million-token context window, and is built for coding and agentic tasks. It is designed to run locally on Apple silicon, with Meta and Apple publicly supporting the collaboration.

segments.title: Local use comes with a high hardware cost
segments.body: Meta says the model can run on two Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra chips, but local use requires substantial memory and computing power. Meta also reports using it for coding work and video-editing tasks. These are company claims and demonstrations, not independent confirmation that it outperforms competing models or performs reliably across everyday workloads.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch highlights the model’s open weights and the possibility of running it locally, while noting that the hardware requirement makes that option accessible mainly to users with high-end machines.

content.headline: Anthropic gives outside researchers employee-level access to assess AI risks
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic gives METR researchers access to assess its AI risks
content.standfirst: Six researchers from nonprofit METR will be able to examine Anthropic’s models, incidents and safety practices, and publish their own assessments. Anthropic can seek limited redactions but cannot veto publication.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access

segments.body: Anthropic says six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI, will receive company laptops, office space and access to internal tools broadly comparable to those used by its own risk-assessment teams. METR will publish its assessments of the company’s models, safety practices and risk management, and Anthropic has agreed not to block publication.

segments.title: Limits on what can be published
segments.body: Anthropic may require redactions in narrowly defined cases, including customer information, legally privileged material or details about model architecture. METR can publicly describe the redactions and say whether it considers them justified, without revealing the withheld information. Anthropic says the arrangement is part of a three-tier evaluation system; METR is the only evaluator currently in its top tier.

content.headline: AI-written job applications are increasing pressure on graduates and employers
content.shortHeadline: AI job applications intensify pressure on graduates and employers
content.standfirst: Some graduates use AI to manage high-volume applications, while employers report suspected misuse in interviews and assessments. Recruiters are trying to balance efficiency with fairness and a genuine sense of candidates’ abilities.

sources.originalTitle: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire

segments.body: Tom, a graduate who applied for more than 200 jobs, says AI helped him tailor CVs and cover letters. A survey of 155 large graduate employers by the Institute of Student Employers found that most were increasingly accepting of some AI use, but 92% had encountered or suspected misconduct, including AI assistance during interviews or online assessments.

segments.title: A contested hiring process
segments.body: Employers say AI-assisted mass applications can increase competition and make it harder to identify candidates’ own skills. EDF’s early-careers recruitment head says the firm closed its graduate scheme early after receiving 12,000 applications, and describes the issue as a moral dilemma for employers and applicants. The survey and interviews reflect reported experiences, not a measure of how often AI use changes hiring outcomes.

content.headline: Meta’s new business terms raise questions about using publishers’ content for AI
content.shortHeadline: Meta terms raise questions about AI training on publishers’ content
content.standfirst: New terms for business accounts appear to permit Meta to crawl associated websites and use their content for AI development and training. Meta says its crawling practices have not changed and disputes the suggestion that the policy targets news sites.

sources.originalTitle: Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free

segments.body: Meta’s commercial terms, due to take effect on 30 October, authorise automated tools to access and collect content from websites associated with business accounts and allow its use to develop, improve and train Meta products. Legal experts told Nieman Lab the wording could affect publishers’ ability to block crawling, but the terms’ practical effect is disputed.

segments.title: Meta disputes the interpretation
segments.body: Meta says the update consolidates existing commercial and advertising terms and that content owners can still use robots.txt instructions. Its communications executives say the change is intended to help with information about products for advertising and recommendations, not to scrape news sites. A Cornell law professor quoted in the report says the terms could nevertheless give Meta permission to train AI on publishers’ material.

perspectives.body: The Verge reports both the legal concern that the terms could override some blocking instructions and Meta’s denial that its crawling practices are changing, leaving the policy’s effect on publishers unsettled.

content.headline: Teacher jailed for creating sexualised AI images of pupils
content.shortHeadline: Teacher jailed for sexualised AI images of pupils
content.standfirst: A former supply teacher in Greater Manchester was jailed for six years after admitting offences including taking indecent photographs of pupils and making sexualised AI images from their social-media photos. The case has renewed calls for stronger action against the creation and spread of such material.

image.caption: Abusali Rahman was jailed after admitting offences involving schoolgirls, including creating sexualised AI images.

sources.originalTitle: Teacher jailed for taking upskirt photos of pupils

segments.body: Abusali Rahman, 37, admitted 21 offences involving girls aged 13 to 16 at seven schools, including taking indecent photographs and creating sexualised AI images from pupils’ social-media photographs. He shared some images online. A judge said Rahman had abused the trust and access afforded by his work as a teacher.

segments.title: Calls for stronger safeguards
segments.body: The NSPCC called for stronger action by technology companies, government and Ofcom to prevent AI-generated sexual images of children being made and shared. Ofcom said providers must assess and mitigate risks under the Online Safety Act, while the government said making or sharing tools intended to generate child sexual abuse material is illegal. The case also involved photographs taken without AI.

content.headline: Patients describe difficulties with an AI receptionist at an Oxfordshire GP
content.shortHeadline: Patients report problems with an AI receptionist at a GP surgery
content.standfirst: Patients at a Wantage practice say an AI call-triage system has caused frustration and, in one case, misunderstood a caller’s reason for contacting the surgery. The practice says feedback has mostly been positive and has introduced an option to speak to a human receptionist.

image.caption: The AI Andi tool screens calls to Newbury Street Practice in Wantage.

sources.originalTitle: Patients' frustration at GP surgery's AI receptionist

segments.body: Newbury Street Practice in Wantage began routing calls through an AI triage tool in July. Some patients told the BBC they struggled to get through to care: one said the system could not help after a 20-minute wait, while another said it thought she was calling about pregnancy. The practice says it now offers callers the option of speaking to a human receptionist.

The surgery says the tool is intended to improve access and free staff to support patients who cannot or do not want to use digital options. It reported that 79% of feedback in the first month was positive, while acknowledging some patients found the change difficult. The report does not establish whether the system has improved access overall.
